parsed.explanation: The combined regime is split: the division is genuinely protective—gender-identity anti-discrimination enforced by a commission, X state IDs, no facility ban, no adult care ban, and a city sanctuary shielding gender-affirming care—but national rules govern every arrival and cannot be overridden locally. Entry screening can flag document/sex discrepancies, refuse admission, and consider lifetime fraud ineligibility; national facilities exclude identity-congruent use; immigration and national custody carry documented abuse and conversion-style treatment. Minors face national care/school hostility, partly offset by local care protections. No execution or general criminalisation of trans identity is documented, and local daily life is comparatively safe. This is Elevated Risk: better than blanket-exclusion border regimes, worse than jurisdictions where border and local systems both protect.

entry_documents.exposure: National visa/passport rules require sex assigned at birth; X markers are not issued; discrepancy or reasonable doubt can trigger refusal, secondary screening, and possible permanent fraud ineligibility; trans athletes are barred. Airport screening can out via scanners or pat-downs.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid until expiry; the policy is challenged in court; a legal-aid FAQ exists. The division offers X state IDs, but those do not control national entry.
entry_documents.interaction: National border officers apply national rules regardless of division anti-discrimination or sanctuary-city limits; local protection begins after admission.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody is documented with forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement, and sexual abuse of trans men; national prisons adopted conversion-style policies involving hair, hormones, and psychiatric drugs, and denied care.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Some executive orders are enjoined; legal challenges are pending; the city sanctuary limits local resources for care investigations, not national custody.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A document discrepancy can move a traveller from border screening into national detention, where local sanctuary and state commission remedies do not bind national custodial staff.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: A national executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity; some states criminalise restroom use, though not this division. National facilities therefore carry exclusion risk.
federal_state_facilities.protection: The division has no facility ban; its largest city requires gender-neutral bathrooms in public buildings and protects nonbinary people; state anti-discrimination covers services.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Local facility protections apply to city and state premises, but national facilities and nationally funded single-sex settings are governed by the national order; the harshest operative rule controls.

care_services.exposure: National orders restrict funding and insurance for minors, describe minor care as mutilation, subpoena hospital records, and proposed rules bar public insurance under 18; national policy chills care.
care_services.protection: The division allows adult gender-affirming surgery and has no adult care ban; the city sanctuary shields gender-affirming care seekers from outside enforcement; municipal conversion-therapy bans and health-board policies apply.
care_services.interaction: Sanctuary protects local care delivery from local enforcement but cannot override national insurance, funding, or investigative authority; adult visitor care is comparatively available, while minor care remains exposed.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy names 'radically pro-transgender' groups among priorities; justice guidance uses 'radical gender ideology'; schools and teachers face investigation for facilitating social transition.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The strategy says counterterrorism powers will not target mere disagreement; courts have enjoined several orders; division anti-discrimination and the human-relations commission operate locally.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: National threat framing raises surveillance or reporting risk for advocacy-linked or visibly trans travellers; local protections do not constrain national counterterrorism or school investigations.

minors_guardians.exposure: National orders treat minor gender-affirming care as mutilation, threaten school funding and prosecution of teachers using preferred names, and proposed rules restrict insurance under 18; 27 states ban care.
minors_guardians.protection: The division has no minor care ban in the dossier; conversion therapy is banned by municipal ordinance and health boards; school-sports bills were vetoed or await lower-chamber action; city youth protections apply.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling minor with a guardian may face national document, care, and school-policy exposure; local care and anti-discrimination protections help inside the division but cannot neutralise national funding, insurance, or school-prosecution policy.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: The state hate-crime statute was struck down and no statewide LGBTQ-inclusive hate-crime law exists; anti-LGBTQ violence falls outside state bias-crime coverage. No documented pattern of trans-targeted street violence in the division.
street_violence_police_response.protection: The national hate-crimes statute covers gender identity; division anti-discrimination law is enforced by the human-relations commission; city ordinances protect trans and nonbinary people.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: National hate-crime recourse exists, but the state-level bias-crime gap weakens local police response; commission remedies cover discrimination, not violence. Street risk is not documented as elevated, but recourse is uneven.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: The passport-marker policy is in litigation; several national orders are enjoined or contested; state protections rest on commission interpretation and regulation, not statute; hate-crime reinstatement and sports bills remain unresolved.
remedies_unknowns.protection: A civil-liberties suit, legal-aid FAQ, human-relations commission remedies including stop orders and damages, a city sanctuary order, and courts blocking some national measures exist.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies may work locally and in court over time, but border and custody decisions are immediate and national; a traveller cannot rely on post-hoc relief to prevent refusal, detention, or facility exclusion.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.25-A describes local police raids, extortion, document checks, and repeat detention with weak courts. This division lacks that local police targeting and has enforced anti-discrimination and a care sanctuary, so it is safer than 0.25-A. But national border screening and national custody abuse remain, so it cannot rise to the mid-range.

0.55-B has extended border secondary screening, humiliation, refusal or return, and slow appeals, but no documented abusive national custody or lifetime fraud finding. Here border screening can escalate to permanent inadmissibility and national detention with documented abuse, so the combined regime is less safe than 0.55-B despite stronger local protections.

0.75-C has trained border officers, brief detention, release, counsel, and compensation; local and border systems largely protect. Here national screening can refuse entry or trigger fraud findings, national facilities exclude identity-congruent use, and custody is abusive; local protections do not reach those stages. Much lower.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime is protective inside the division but exposed at the national gate. Anti-discrimination, X state IDs, city sanctuary, and local care access reduce everyday risk for an adult visitor and a travelling family. However, national border screening, document rules, facility exclusion, and custodial practices sit above the division and are not pre-empted or refused by local actors. The harshest operative rule governs: refusal or lifetime inadmissibility at entry, and abusive national custody if detention follows. Local protections cannot cancel those national exposures, though they materially improve life after admission. This places the jurisdiction in Elevated Risk rather than Reduced Risk.
